title: AI could substantially accelerate AI research
claim: AI systems can substantially increase the effective rate of AI research and development across a meaningful portion of the frontier-model R&D process, rather than merely assisting isolated tasks.

supportingEvidence.name: OpenAI — Research acceleration
supportingEvidence.summary: OpenAI reports that its research organization now uses about 3.1 agent-workdays for every human workday. Researchers are contributing code faster, running more experiments, delegating increasingly complex work, and report that agentic tools are meaningfully accelerating research progress.

supportingEvidence.name: Anthropic — R&D Automation Index
supportingEvidence.summary: Anthropic reports Claude at 'collaborates' level or above for more than 90% of measured AI R&D work and at 'leads' level for 26%, up from under 1% in February 2026. No measured subset is yet fully autonomous.

supportingEvidence.name: METR — Claude Opus 5.5 evaluation
supportingEvidence.summary: Independent evaluation concludes that the model is likely to noticeably accelerate researchers and automate limited aspects of R&D, while still showing important weaknesses on long-horizon work and researcher judgement.

supportingEvidence.name: Chan et al. — Automating AI R&D and intelligence explosion
supportingEvidence.summary: A multi-author assessment concludes that AI R&D automation is advancing rapidly and that preliminary evidence makes substantial acceleration plausible, while emphasizing large uncertainty about the magnitude and downstream dynamics.

limitations: The strongest evidence is still concentrated in component activities such as coding, infrastructure troubleshooting, experiment execution and analysis. OpenAI explicitly notes that faster code generation and more experiments are imperfect proxies for overall research progress and that compute, judgement, prioritization and other less-automatable tasks can become bottlenecks. Anthropic's measurements are internal and partly model-judged, and its index shows no fully autonomous R&D subset. METR reports that current frontier models still have qualitative weaknesses in foresight, open-ended reasoning, creating feedback loops and researcher judgement, and says available data cannot yet distinguish accelerating from constant or decelerating improvement. Independent analyses also note that recent benchmark trends do not yet clearly show a broad acceleration in frontier capability growth attributable to AI R&D automation.
assessment: Emerging — moderate confidence. Evidence has moved beyond isolated assistance: frontier labs report large and rapidly increasing AI participation in real AI R&D workflows, higher experiment throughput and delegation of increasingly complex tasks, while independent evaluation expects noticeable researcher acceleration. But the proposition concerns substantial acceleration of the overall research process. Current evidence does not yet cleanly measure how much faster frontier capabilities advance because of AI assistance, and important human, compute, evaluation and judgement bottlenecks remain. The evidence therefore supports a strengthening Emerging classification rather than Established.
changeTest: Upgrade to Established if independent or auditable longitudinal evidence shows a large causal increase in end-to-end AI R&D output or frontier capability progress attributable to AI systems — for example, comparable teams or development cycles producing materially more validated advances per unit time because of AI automation. Downgrade would be warranted if better controlled studies show that apparent gains in coding and experiment throughput are largely offset by verification, integration, compute or judgement bottlenecks and do not materially accelerate validated research progress.

additionalSources.name: IFP — Preparing for increasingly automated AI R&D

history.note: Initial full evidence review published. Classification retained at Emerging · Moderate confidence; evidence strengthened substantially, especially for component-level R&D acceleration, while end-to-end acceleration remains insufficiently measured.
